page: Amazon Web Services c8id.xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor running at 3.9 GHz. Built on the x86_64 architecture and managed by the Nitro hypervisor, this server features 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The hardware configuration includes 8.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 7 GHz, yielding a memory-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per core. For local storage, the instance is equipped with a 237 GB NVMe SSD, while network connectivity is provisioned at a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps. The CPU architecture supports advanced instruction sets, including Intel Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX-512) and Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for accelerated matrix operations.

Benchmark data reveals strong single-core performance, with a Geekbench single-core score of 2202.0 and high single-threaded throughput in gzip compression (34.39 GB/sec) and bzip3 decompression (14.52 GB/sec). However, multi-core scaling presents a notable tradeoff. The stress-ng multi-core CPU performance and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression fall into the lower 25th percentile, reflecting the physical limitation of its 2-core design. Memory performance is mixed; while large-block read and write bandwidths are average, the Passmark memory score and small-block cached read bandwidth are relatively weak. For specialized workloads, the onboard AMX capabilities support moderate AI inference, achieving 34.58 tokens per second for prompt processing on medium 7B models, though text generation on the same model drops to a poor 4.81 tokens per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the c8id.xlarge offers a dense compute profile with high-speed DDR5 memory and integrated NVMe storage, reducing the need for external storage attachments for transient data. This resource balance makes the instance suitable for single-threaded compute tasks, lightweight web serving, and software compilation. It is also appropriate for database operations and key-value stores like Redis, where the local NVMe SSD and average database benchmark performance can be leveraged effectively without requiring massive memory footprints.
